title: Making Your Rivals Depend on Your System Is How America Has Won for Three Centuries
dek: The Dutch, the British and the Americans took turns as hegemon not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake their survival on someone else's maritime order — once they can't live without the sea lanes and the markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective weapon short of war.
why: Walter Mead breaks America's three-hundred-year winning streak into a five-step strategy and pushes it all the way to China, the Taiwan Strait and AI deterrence. What you get is a durable framework for judgment, not news-cycle opinion.
who: Founders going overseas and anyone working in US-China supply chains, engineers studying the Taiwan Strait or the drone revolution in warfare, investors watching AI policy risk.

points.h: Unpredictability is a form of power
points.body: ‘Unpredictability’ is not madness; it is a modern strategy of power. Mead says post-Cold War American diplomacy held itself up as a pillar of stability by ‘letting the whole world know where America's red lines are’, while Trump profits by doing the opposite: crossing lines, threatening allies, turning commitments into bargaining chips. He saw through a secret of the information age — the marginal cost of lying: the first lie is expensive, the thousandth is nearly free. When Clinton was engulfed by the Lewinsky scandal, he discovered that shame only lives in other people's minds; as long as you keep walking, the dogs bark but the caravan moves on. Trump took that insight to industrial scale. The cost is borne by the American diplomatic system: when the world's number one power turns itself into the unpredictable card, every alliance and rule built on predictability after World War II is coming apart faster.

points.h: The last step of global hegemony is cutting the cord
points.body: The Anglo-American maritime order did not win through some single battle but through a five-step playbook: first, an open society on an island — the seventeenth-century Dutch tolerated heretics and Jews, and ideas and capital poured in; then global trade, with Dutch merchant ships sailing the world, so wealthy that even their paintings are full of Turkish carpets and Brazilian parrots; third, while continental powers fought over inland Silesia, you seized India and Canada across the globe. The fourth step is the riskiest: instead of copying Spain and sealing off your colonies, you invite the whole world in to do business, the British navy suppresses pirates, and every merchant ship benefits; Germany and Japan were likewise invited in after the war. Only the last step is the hole card: once the other side cannot do without your grain, your rubber and your shipping lanes, you cut it off — Germany discovered in World War I that Argentine grain and Malayan rubber had all been cut off, and its economy promptly seized up.

points.h: Everything China does is to avoid having the cord cut
points.body: Look at China through the same framework and you find Beijing is well aware of its own jugular. Mead says: suppose the mainland blockades Taiwan, and the US counter-blockades from a hundred miles off Taiwan's coast: oil cannot get in, manufactured goods cannot get out, soybean contracts with Brazil and Argentina are voided, and China's economy is strangled alive. He has discussed these things with officials and scholars at Chinese universities, and this worry is always present. So China's energy policy has to be read side by side: on one hand building oil reserves so large they surprise outsiders; on the other, throwing up solar and hydropower while digging as much coal as possible. It is not schizophrenia, it is the same thing: pulling out, one by one, the soft spots of ‘dependence on the outside world’. He also warns the US not to retreat into isolationism — agriculture and AI both need overseas markets to feed themselves.

points.h: Every round of technology dividends needs new institutions to match
points.body: Mead starts from the ownership society: at America's founding there were independent farmers with land everywhere, and while a bridge is a fine thing, it means raising my taxes — that trade-off is itself a political education. The railroad era was matched by the Homestead Act, with the government giving land to railroad companies and farmers, and a national market grew out of it; in the twentieth century what replaced the family farm was the single-family suburban house, paired with tax-exempt municipal bonds and highways, becoming a new machine for distributing wealth. Today that machine has run into housing prices: young people cannot afford to live near where they work. His remedy is remote work and autonomous driving. When the commuting radius expands from 40 miles to 75 miles, usable land for housing rises with the square of the radius, and the physical space opened by technology is enough to carry two more generations. But the precondition is filling in the institutional ‘infrastructure’ — he coined the word info-structure, meaning the institutions and regulatory rules that let AI actually land in hospitals and courts.

points.h: Silicon Valley is defecting to the tech Hamiltonians
points.body: American foreign policy debate has for centuries been four vocabularies: Hamiltonians want a strong state clearing the way for capital, Wilsonians want to spread liberal democracy, Jeffersonians fear a bigger government, Jacksonians stay isolationist in peacetime and fight to the death when hit. The post-Cold War establishment was a marriage of Hamilton and Wilson, but Trump brought Jefferson and Jackson into the room. Mead says the genuinely noteworthy new species is the Tech Hamiltonian. In the 1990s tech companies loved to say ‘we are a global company, Google has no borders, Washington has no jurisdiction’; AI competition has turned tech into a contest of national destiny. Economic positions changed too: the old multinational car companies wanted borderless labor and markets, while Silicon Valley wants supply-chain and IP security, and even wants its employees patriotic — selling code to China is shameful, and your colleagues will report you outright. The core of business has shifted from the old multinationals to tech nationalists, and this is the underwater current of America's political realignment.

points.h: The power with more equipment fears technological turnover most
points.body: Mead has been to Ukraine twice. The first time, at a drone factory, he saw them converting children's toy trucks into ground drones carrying mines to blow up tanks; months later, the progress was unimaginably fast. The battlefield is now a gray kill zone, usually only two or three soldiers operating together, and one of the hardest problems is ‘how to get the wounded out’ — you need to build a ground drone with a metal shield to drag people, with a squad of drones alongside to hunt the enemy drones coming to attack it. He heard of one wounded soldier who took 63 days to be evacuated from the front. The changes flip every six months. The bitterest irony for the US: the power with the most tanks and aircraft carriers is precisely the one that fears this kind of parameter revolution most — existing equipment turns from an advantage into a relocation cost. Russia's Black Sea Fleet has no great battle to fight, yet it is bottled up at home by Ukrainian small boats and drones.

points.h: The new variable most worth watching in the Taiwan Strait is Japan
points.body: On whether the mainland will attack Taiwan, Mead's judgment is that Beijing needs a very high probability of success before it is willing to cross the threshold — failure would be catastrophic for the initiator. But between ‘attack’ and ‘do nothing’ there is a long gray ladder: for example, requiring all merchant ships bound for Taiwan to first call at mainland ports for customs clearance, or imposing a soft blockade — actions sufficient to change facts on the ground without triggering an armed US response. The real new variable on the Taiwan board is not America's attitude but Japan. The Japanese have already publicly concluded that if China takes Taiwan, Japanese independence is finished too; they are raising defense budgets, rewriting security doctrine and reshaping the national psyche. Historically Japan turns very fast when faced with a real threat. How steep Japan's learning curve is, and whether Beijing's calculations must factor Japan in, is the key to the Taiwan question in the coming years.

points.h: AI actually makes deterrence more credible
points.body: Moving Cold War deterrence logic into the algorithmic age, Mead points to a counterintuitive corollary: deterrence succeeds or fails on making the opponent one hundred percent believe that ‘if I do X, you will necessarily do Y, and you can do it and are willing to’. As long as there is a human veto point in the decision chain — ‘I might go soft when the time comes’ — that commitment has a crack in it. Automating part of foreign-policy decision-making and handing it to AI turns retaliation into an executable mechanism that will not hesitate — and deterrence becomes more credible. But this is the doomsday machine problem from science fiction: decisions of civilizational scale no longer require a human to bear the consequences. His own assessment of the question is that it is ‘very interesting and also a bit confusing’, and he does not think the answer has appeared yet.

terms.def: A new force in American foreign policy that wants state power to clear the way for tech companies, replacing the old free-market multinational capital.
The institutions, laws and regulatory frameworks needed for AI to land safely in hospitals, courts and similar settings, as distinct from physical infrastructure.
The American hawkish tradition of paying no attention to the outside world in peacetime and destroying the enemy with full force once attacked.
A way of applying pressure without going directly to war, slowly strangling the other side's trade through customs, insurance and port rules.
